fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Archetypes Flattened to One Dimension", "body": "Chance frames the game's card descriptions as archetypes reduced to a single dimension, when anyone who reads tarot knows a card can mean many things depending on context. In his view the artificial future wants circuitry with a predictable pathway. Lindsey reads the cyber Justice figure as judge, jury, and executioner rather than the detached observer the sword is meant to signal, and she notes the towers have lost their sense of tradition. Later Chance names the pattern outright, reduction of humanity and reduction of archetypes, while noting that alchemical reduction carries a gentler meaning."}, {"title": "Transactional Balance Versus Natural Flow", "body": "Chance argues that one of the biggest ways society moved into artificiality was by de-spiritualizing number and making everything transactional. He points to indigenous cultures where matching a gift's value is taboo because it cancels the bond, and he contrasts that with a commerce mind trying to extract a little more than equal. Real balance, he says, is a big free flow of energy where nobody keeps score. Lindsey ties this to words as an artificial layer and adds that tipped scales can be a good thing, since imbalance is how energy keeps moving."}, {"title": "The Hanged Man and the Crowd", "body": "Lindsey notes that in her own deck the Hanged Man is Odin, a sacrifice made by choice for the sake of others, while the cyber version looks strung up in a web, a dark ritual put upon him. Chance wonders whether the skull-faced figure is the Magician caught with his face off, and reads the corporate suit as the costume of a sacrifice with no meaning. He credits crowd psychology with letting people dodge responsibility by saying the group did it, and contrasts that with Odin and Jesus, who act rightly despite the crowd."}, {"title": "Death, the Machine, and the Sacred Clown", "body": "Lindsey observes that the Death card's text sounds balanced while its art is all terror and brutality, with a figure wired into the machine rather than a gentle ferryman. Chance goes further and calls the machine itself death, arguing that whatever we hand to technology is a part of ourselves we eventually kill, and Lindsey agrees that every convenience replaces something we once did for ourselves. Chance also raises the heyoka, a clown-like figure in Native American tribes who breaks taboos to poke at cracks in the ego, as a positive trickster role, while Lindsey insists this Death is brutality for its own sake."}, {"title": "Addiction, Choice, and Self-Existing Nature", "body": "Lindsey says that when the Devil appears in a reading she treats it as a temptation that always offers a choice and a chance to purify, while the cyber Devil is pure response with no structure. Chance notes that the original chains hang loose enough to remove, and offers a wordplay of his own, that addiction is a story added over the story of yourself. He then argues the artificial figure will burn out because it cannot reproduce, calls himself an anti-creationist, and says nature is self-existing, a point Lindsey likens to dependent arising in Buddhism."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Lindsey Scharmyn of Rogue Ways had me on her show to finish up the analysis of the Transhuman Tarot from Cyberpunk 2077. The latter half of the Major Arcana were definitely as deep as the first, and it's always fascinating to follow that legendary Path of the Fool on another journey, albeit a dark one this time around.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: You'll want to watch the video version of this episode so you can follow along with the slide images we're looking at. The extended version completes the analysis of all the Major Arcana cards.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Tower, Babel, and the Missing Foundation", "body": "Lindsey welcomes the Tower, saying she wants the lightning to come, since a structure that falls needed rebuilding and one that stands is proven sound. She argues the cyber tower has no foundation, so the lightning rips through the whole scene instead of being grounded. Chance reads the data-center tower as the Tower of Babel, a mountain of collected knowledge that could be wiped out, and sees big data as a corruption of language because all of it runs on code. He adds a plot point from the game itself, a corporate tower destroyed in the city."}, {"title": "Artificial Time and Internal Sovereignty", "body": "Chance describes a fake Kronos time, the rat race and hamster wheel, and points out that every database entry needs a timestamp, so a digital identity is like a cartoon, images put in order to create the illusion of life. Lindsey adds that a threat only becomes actionable once it carries a time. Chance says he recently learned Sargon of Akkad is credited with inventing time, and both describe following an internal synchronicity compass. Chance argues that the more internal sovereignty you have, the more external things are anarchical."}, {"title": "Celebrity, Pedestals, and Intention Over Hope", "body": "On the Star card Chance sees the inversion as Hollywood's treatment of the archetype, a holographic figure with imitative smaller stars watching, and he says nobody benefits from a pedestal relationship because someone is always on the pedestal and someone in the pit. He calls the original tarot biophilic and the cyber tarot necrophilic. He distinguishes intention, which requires courage, from hope, which he says implies passivity. Lindsey describes a third kind of hope that acts well and hopes the ripples spread, and Chance replies that trusting yourself lets you trust the universe."}, {"title": "Moon, Sun, and the Mars Question", "body": "Lindsey loves the Moon for its potent manifestation energy when emotion and vision are handled with structure, but the cyber version strikes her as pure illusion and trap, its light caged behind fencing. Chance points to the data ocean replacing water, a skull where the scorpion belonged, and the missing sun. On the Sun card Lindsey reads an egotistical pose, a figure saying look at me, and says the cracked orb looks like Mars. Chance wonders aloud whether the card is hinting at Mars, while Lindsey cautions that symbols appearing in a certain order do not prove the maker is in the know or in a secret group."}, {"title": "Judgment, the World, and Art Against Artifice", "body": "Lindsey reads the cyber Judgment angel as a Cthulhu-esque judge with a hidden hand behind it, the opposite of a call to self-realization. Chance says this system eats you at your strongest, yet insists every act was witnessed by you. On the World card Lindsey says the figure took the elevator down and became everything made of circuits and death, and Chance calls it the dark singularity, a warning rather than glorification. Late on, Chance argues all evil is artificial, and Lindsey adds that nothing real and true can be lost."}]

So if you feel like you've lost it, it never existed in the first place. It was an illusion and a distraction.", "author": "Lindsey Scharmyn", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/266fc9f2-e364-4218-b441-a558779d7c0c/LINDSAY-SCHARMYN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "A big difference between children and adults is that adults have become so good at pretending that they're not pretending that they forgot that they're pretending.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "One of the biggest ways that society has moved into artificiality is to completely de-spiritualize number a hundred percent and make everything transactional.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Sometimes the scales are tipped, and that's like a good thing because that's how energy moves.", "author": "Lindsey Scharmyn", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/266fc9f2-e364-4218-b441-a558779d7c0c/LINDSAY-SCHARMYN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Everything that we give to the machine to have it do for us, that part of ourself we've killed eventually.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You're supposed to be transmuting your inner self and your inner world and you're supposed to be crystallizing those aspects of yourself that are the most pure and the most true.", "author": "Lindsey Scharmyn", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/266fc9f2-e364-4218-b441-a558779d7c0c/LINDSAY-SCHARMYN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I'm seeing a definite theme of the reduction here. Reduction of humanity, reduction of archetypes to one dimension.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The devil looks dark and scary, but it's actually offering us all of this growth and this opportunity if we take it that way.", "author": "Lindsey Scharmyn", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/266fc9f2-e364-4218-b441-a558779d7c0c/LINDSAY-SCHARMYN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You don't have any reckonable beginning.
